<!--
PSYCH 251 replication report template.

Every project uses this structure so that reports are comparable across the class. They
become public supplementary material, so write for a reader who has the original paper but
not your repository.

The project has two phases, and so does this report:
  Phase 1, the replication. Introduction and Methods are written, critiqued and preregistered
           BEFORE data collection; the Methods addendum, Results and Discussion after it.
  Phase 2, the extension. Proposed after Phase 1 (Rationale, Changes from Phase 1, Power and
           sample, Analysis plan), then run, with its own Results and Discussion.
The AI use statement and the Key statistics table sit at the top and are kept current
throughout. Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas for Phase 2.

Render this file at every stage. Before a phase has data, its results say so and skip
themselves; during Pilot A the Phase 1 results run on pilot data, which is the point of Pilot A.

Grey "Guidance" boxes are instructions. Delete each one once you have written that section.
The code is wired to the template's demo experiment (the framing problem). Replace the demo

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)   # includes ggplot2
library(jsonlite)
library(psych)       # descriptive statistics (also used by the original authors)
library(apaTables)   # APA-style correlation table (also used by the original authors)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "osborne2026-pilot-a"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "osborne2026-phase2"

# PILOT SWITCH. TRUE = Pilot A: the testers did not have to be women over 40, so we only
# require "completed" and "assigned to normal or distress", and the model is allowed to run
# with as few as 8 people. FALSE = the real study: the full exclusion rule is applied and
# at least 20 people are needed. Set this to FALSE before the real data collection.
pilot_mode <- TRUE
min_n      <- if (pilot_mode) 8 else 20
# In pilot mode the model has no control variables (see fit_outcome), so the caption says so.
model_note <- if (pilot_mode) "no control variables in the pilot model" else
  "controlling for age, education, social media use and menopause stage"
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figure.
# Source: Osborne, Brown & Sillence (2026), JMIR Formative Research, 10:e85788.
#
# Sample: 749 people took part; 4 + 8 were excluded, so N = 737 were analysed.
# Groups: normal = 248, distress = 241, transformative = 248.
orig_n <- c(normal = 248, distress = 241, transformative = 248)

# Ordinal logistic regression results for "distress vs normal" (the comparison group is
# normal). beta = log-odds coefficient (the effect size), se = its standard error,
# z = beta / se. Outcomes were rated on a 5-point scale.
original <- tribble(
  ~outcome,       ~beta,   ~se,    ~z,
  "worried",       0.910,  0.170,  5.350,
  "reassured",    -0.970,  0.167, NA,
  "confused",      0.818,  0.170, NA,
  "optimistic",   -0.708,  0.165, NA,
  "anxious",       0.817,  0.168, NA,
  "empowered",    -0.540,  0.162, NA,
  "knowledgeable", 0.564,  0.163, NA,
  "liked",        -0.864,  0.171, NA
)
# Our key analysis: worried, distress vs normal.
original_key <- original |> filter(outcome == "worried")
```

# Key statistics

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your
Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the
analysis code below (open "Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are
analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design and preregistered
exclusion rule. On the scientific-extension track, the Phase 2 row reports the new comparison:
adapt its code and say so in the caption.


```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# ---- shared analysis code (goes in the analysis-functions chunk) ----

# Turn one survey page's answers into columns. jsPsych saves each page's answers as one JSON
# string, for example {"worried":2,"reassured":1,...}. This unpacks that string for one task.
parse_task <- function(trials, task_name) {
  one <- trials |> filter(task == task_name)
  if (nrow(one) == 0) return(tibble(participant_id = character()))
  one |>
    mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
    select(participant_id, resp) |>
    unnest_wider(resp)
}

# The 5 answer choices of the social media use question, in order (Never = 1 ... Several times
# per day = 5). Used to turn the answer into a number for the model.
social_levels <- c("Never", "Less than weekly", "Weekly", "Daily", "Several times per day")

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # Keep only people who finished the study, and compute how many minutes they took
  # (end time minus start time; the times are saved as text like 2026-10-15T22:29:55Z).
  complete <- participants |>
    filter(completed) |>
    mutate(minutes = as.numeric(difftime(lubridate::ymd_hms(ended_at),
                                         lubridate::ymd_hms(started_at), units = "mins")))

  # One row per completed participant: condition, demographics, and every rating.
  # jsPsych saves the 5-point answers as 0-4, so 1 is added to put them back on 1-5.
  tr <- trials |> filter(participant_id %in% complete$participant_id)
  rating_cols <- c("liked", "credible", "trust", "empowered", "knowledgeable",
                   "worried", "reassured", "confused", "in_control", "optimistic", "anxious")
  dat <- complete |>
    select(participant_id, condition, minutes) |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "demographics"), by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "ratings_agree"), by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "ratings_feel"), by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(
      across(any_of(rating_cols), ~ as.numeric(.x) + 1),
      age                 = as.numeric(age),
      education_years     = as.numeric(education_years),
      social_media_use    = match(social_media_use, social_levels),
      condition           = factor(condition, levels = c("normal", "distress"))
    )

  # Exclusion rule (the same one written in the Analysis plan). We KEEP a person only if:
  #  - they were assigned to normal or distress (the pilot also had a third group, which is
  #    now NA and is dropped),
  #  - they are 40 or older,
  #  - they said they are in perimenopause or postmenopause,
  #  - they took at least 2.5 minutes (the original study's rule),
  #  - they report 20 or fewer years of education after age 16.
  # (People who did not complete the study were already removed above.)
  # In pilot mode (see the pilot switch at the top) the age, menopause, time and education
  # rules are skipped, because Pilot A testers did not have to be eligible women.
  # (A completed session with no worry rating, for example an old test session, cannot be
  # analysed, so it is also dropped.)
  keep <- dat |> filter(!is.na(condition), !is.na(worried))
  if (!pilot_mode) {
    keep <- keep |>
      filter(age >= 40,
             menopause_stage %in% c("peri", "post"),
             minutes >= 2.5,
             education_years <= 20)
  }

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, dat = dat, keep = keep,
       n_not_menopausal = sum(dat$menopause_stage %in% "not"))
}

# Fit the ordinal logistic regression for ONE outcome (for example "worried"): the rating
# predicted by condition (normal is the comparison group) plus the four control variables.
# Returns one row per non-normal condition, or NULL if the model cannot be fitted yet
# (for example while there are only a few pilot participants).
fit_outcome <- function(dat, outcome) {
  d <- dat |>
    select(all_of(outcome), condition, age, education_years, social_media_use, menopause_stage) |>
    rename(y = all_of(outcome)) |>
    drop_na() |>
    mutate(y = factor(y, ordered = TRUE), condition = droplevels(condition))
  # The model: condition plus the four control variables. In pilot mode there are too few
  # people for four extra variables (the model cannot find a solution with about 10 rows),
  # so the pilot model uses condition only. The real study uses the full model.
  model_formula <- if (pilot_mode) y ~ condition else
    y ~ condition + age + education_years + social_media_use + menopause_stage
  if (nrow(d) < min_n || nlevels(d$condition) < 2 || nlevels(d$y) < 2) return(NULL)
  m <- tryCatch(
    MASS::polr(model_formula, data = d, Hess = TRUE),
    error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  broom::tidy(m) |>
    filter(coef.type == "coefficient", startsWith(term, "condition")) |>
    transmute(outcome = outcome,
              contrast = sub("^condition", "", term),
              N = nrow(d),
              beta = estimate, se = std.error, z = statistic,
              p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(statistic)),
              ci_low = beta - 1.96 * se, ci_high = beta + 1.96 * se)
}

# The key statistic: worried, distress vs normal. NULL until the model can be fitted.
key_result <- function(d) {
  r <- fit_outcome(d$keep, "worried")
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  r |> filter(contrast == "distress")
}

# All the secondary outcomes with the same model, distress vs normal.
outcomes <- c("worried", "reassured", "confused", "optimistic", "anxious",
              "empowered", "knowledgeable", "liked")
all_results <- function(d) {
  res <- map_dfr(outcomes, function(o) {
    r <- fit_outcome(d$keep, o)
    if (is.null(r)) tibble() else r
  })
  if (nrow(res) == 0) return(NULL)
  res |> filter(contrast == "distress")
}

# Side-by-side figure: the effect (beta, distress vs normal) with its 95% interval for each
# outcome, original and replication on the same axes. Positive = distress group rated higher.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(ci_low = beta - 1.96 * se, ci_high = beta + 1.96 * se,
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           outcome = factor(outcome, levels = rev(outcomes)))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  ggplot(df, aes(x = outcome, y = beta, colour = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Effect of distress vs normal (ordinal logistic β, 95% CI)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `β` = "not yet collected", SE = "",
                  `95% CI` = "", z = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `β` = sprintf("%.3f", r$beta), SE = sprintf("%.3f", r$se),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         z = sprintf("%.2f", r$z),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
original_row <- original_key |>
  transmute(N = sum(orig_n), beta, se, z, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)),
            ci_low = beta - 1.96 * se, ci_high = beta + 1.96 * se)
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", original_row),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) key_result(phase1)),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) key_result(phase2))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
               caption = paste0("Key comparison: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry (ordinal logistic regression, ", model_note, ")."))
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

The original study found that showing social media posts to peri- and postmenopausal women framing the menopause transition as either normal, distressful, or transformative had immediate effects on affective responses (Osborne et al., 2026). Participants who viewed distress-framed posts reported greater levels of worry and confusion, and lower levels of reassurance, optimism, and empowerment. Interestingly, the distress-framed posts increased perceived knowledge of menopause, despite participants feeling more negatively toward them. I replicated the study with only two conditions (normal vs distress) to examine the original study’s main finding, the same affective reactions, expected behavioral responses, and perceptions scales were utilized. This study was important for me because it demonstrates how narrative framing shapes affective responses and the importance of choosing the right words to share medical information, especially for a stage of life that half of the population will live through for almost 40% of their lives. Negative framing could also affect how women experience their symptoms physically. I would like to further investigate the mind-body effects of menopausal mindsets in the future.

One challenge that I anticipated was obtaining the original materials from the authors, but they shared their original posts with me. For the statistical analysis, I used ordinal logistic regression for each ordinal outcome, comparing the distress condition with the normal condition.

For the extension, I planned to include a brief message to reframe how menopause is presented in the posts.

## Methods

### Power analysis

```{r}
#| label: power
# The original effect (beta) is on the "log-odds" scale. A logistic distribution has a
# standard deviation of pi / sqrt(3), so beta divided by that number gives an approximate
# Cohen's d, which the usual t-test power calculation can use. This is an approximation:
# it ignores the control variables.
d_orig <- original_key$beta / (pi / sqrt(3))

# The original study used p < .01, so power is calculated for alpha = .01.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = d_orig, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.01, power = pw)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 2 * ceiling(n))
})

# 2.5 times the original sample in the two groups of the key test (normal and distress).
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * orig_n[c("normal", "distress")])

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per condition", "N total"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect on worry (beta = %.3f, about d = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .01, two conditions (normal vs distress).",
               original_key$beta, d_orig))
```

```{r}
#| label: power-proposed
# How much power does the sample I plan to collect have? The first row uses the original
# effect. The other rows ask "what if the true effect is smaller than the original?",
# because original effects are often overestimates.
proposed_per_group <- 130   # my planned N per condition (change this if the plan changes)

power_check <- tibble(
  effect = c("Original effect", "75% of the original", "Half of the original"),
  d      = d_orig * c(1, 0.75, 0.5)
) |>
  mutate(
    # power.t.test() with n filled in (and power left out) returns the power
    power = map_dbl(d, ~ power.t.test(n = proposed_per_group, delta = .x,
                                      sd = 1, sig.level = 0.01)$power),
    d     = round(d, 2),
    power = scales::percent(power, accuracy = 1)
  )

knitr::kable(power_check,
             col.names = c("True effect", "Cohen's d", "Power"),
             caption = sprintf("Power of %d participants per condition (alpha = .01) if the true effect is as large as, or smaller than, the original.",
                               proposed_per_group))
```

The original effect for the worry question comparing the distress and normal conditions was β = .910, which was converted to a Cohen’s d of about 0.50 using the template’s code.

For an alpha of .01, a minimum of 120 participants per condition was needed for 90% power to detect the original effect.

I chose 130 participants per group because of resource constraints, which gave around 93% power to detect the original effect. However, the true effect could be smaller than the effect found in the original study.

### Planned sample

A sample of 260 women 40 years or older who are perimenopausal or postmenopausal was recruited through Prolific.

Recruitment stopped when data from 260 people who passed the inclusion/exclusion criteria had been collected.

### Materials

The original study used 12 social media posts, with four posts for each narrative: normal, distress, and transformative. This replication study used only the original posts from the normal and distress conditions. Each participant saw four posts from their assigned condition. The study included basic sociodemographic questions and questions about menopause stage, HRT experience, perceived menopause knowledge, and social media use. After viewing the posts, participants answered the original questions about their affective responses, expected behavioral responses, and perceptions of the posts.

Materials available at the following link: https://psych251.github.io/osborne2026/

### Procedure

Participants recruited through Prolific were directed to a consent page to participate in the study and then answered basic sociodemographic and clinical questions about their menopause. After that, they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (normal/distress), in which they were instructed to view four posts framing menopause as either a distressing or a "normal" experience. The social media posts from the original study were shared by the authors to use in this replication study. The posts were anonymized, standardized, and copied from public X, Instagram, and Facebook posts. The participants answered questions about the message of the posts, how the posts made them feel (worried, reassured, confused, optimistic), their behavioral intentions (like, share, save, comment, search, discuss), and their perceptions of the posts (likability, credibility, trustworthiness, representativeness). The original question sequence was followed, but only with the two groups (normal and distress posts) instead of three, because of resource constraints. The transformative posts were not included. The experiment was run on a jsPsych website instead of Qualtrics.

### Analysis plan

As in the original study, statistical analyses were done using R. The packages apaTables, ggplot2, psych, and tidyverse were used for data processing, analysis, and visualization.

Participant characteristics, HRT experience, perceived menopause knowledge, and social media engagement were described using descriptive statistics. Categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages. Continuous variables were presented as means, SDs, and ranges. Ordinal logistic regression was used because the outcomes were measured on ordered 5-point Likert-type scales. The models examined the impact of experimental condition on affective, behavioral, and perceptual responses to the posts, using the normal narrative condition as the reference category. Models controlled for age, years of education after age 16, menopause stage, and frequency of social media use. Following the original authors, P < .01 was used as the significance threshold because several outcomes were tested.

**Key analysis of interest.** My key analysis of interest was to compare worry ratings between the distress and normal conditions using ordinal logistic regression. In the original study, compared to participants who viewed posts portraying menopause as normal, those who viewed distress posts reported to be more worried about menopause (β = .910; SE = .170; Wald z = 5.350; P < .001; Osborne et al., 2026).

The test was an ordinal logistic regression of the worry likert question on condition. The effect size was β (log-odds) for distress vs normal, with a 95% confidence interval.

**Secondary outcomes.** Feeling reassured, confused, optimistic, anxious, empowered, and knowledgeable, and how much participants liked the posts, were also examined using the same ordinal logistic regression model and covariates.

**Exclusions.** Participants were excluded if they did not complete the study, completed the survey in less than 2.5 minutes, or reported more than 20 years of education after age 16. The original research team considered less than 2.5 minutes insufficient time to read and process the survey content.

Participants were also excluded if they were not perimenopausal or postmenopausal women. Participants younger than 40 years old were also excluded.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Number of groups | 3 (normal, distress, transformative) | 2 (normal, distress) | No, because the primary outcome of the replication study is the distress vs normal posts. |
| Platform | Qualtrics | jsPsych website | Not probable. The questions, posts, and their sequence are the same. |
| Sample size | 737 participants were analyzed, about 245 per group. | About 260 (130 per group) | Not probable. The estimated power for my sample was approximately 93% to detect the study’s original effect (d = .50). |
| Sample and pay | Prolific, UK women 40+, peri or postmenopausal, paid £1.50 | Prolific, same type of women; it is not guaranteed that they will be from the UK. Paid about $8 per hour. | Not probable, as long as they meet the inclusion criteria. |
| 60-second wait | A timer stopped people from moving on | The Continue button is locked for 60 seconds, with a bold instruction sentence, because in the pilot people missed the instruction and thought it was a website problem. | Not probable, it avoids the problem of the participants thinking the website is broken, it's not supposed to influence their responses. |

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Completed", "Passed exclusion criteria")
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Started"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed"),
  keep         |> mutate(step = "Passed exclusion criteria")
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels)) |>
  count(step, condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by frame. Differences between frames in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")
```

```{r}
#| label: descriptives
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Descriptive statistics for the analysed sample, with the same packages the original authors
# named: psych (summary table) and apaTables (APA-style correlation table).
if (nrow(keep) > 2) {
  vars <- keep |> select(age, education_years, social_media_use, worried) |>
    mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

  # psych::describe() gives n, mean, SD, min and max for every column in one line.
  psych::describe(vars)[, c("n", "mean", "sd", "min", "max")] |>
    round(2) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Descriptive statistics of the analysed sample.")

  # apaTables::apa.cor.table() builds the correlation table; filename = NA means "do not
  # save a Word file, just give me the table". tryCatch keeps the report from stopping if
  # the pilot is too small to compute correlations.
  tryCatch(
    knitr::kable(apaTables::apa.cor.table(vars, filename = NA)$table.body,
                 caption = "Means, SDs and correlations (APA style)."),
    error = function(e) cat("Correlation table not available yet (too few participants).\n"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: categorical-descriptives
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Counts and percentages for the categorical variables (the Analysis plan says categorical
# variables are reported this way). A small helper does the same job for each variable.
count_pct <- function(d, var) {
  d |>
    count(Level = .data[[var]]) |>                      # how many people gave each answer
    mutate(Percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1),        # n divided by the total, times 100
           Variable = var, .before = 1)
}
if (nrow(keep) > 0) {
  bind_rows(count_pct(keep, "menopause_stage"),
            count_pct(keep, "hrt"),
            count_pct(keep, "knowledge"),
            count_pct(keep, "condition")) |>
    rename(N = n) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Counts and percentages for the categorical variables (analysed sample).")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: pilot-worry-plot
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-height: 3.5
# Pilot-only figure: average worry in each condition, with a 95% interval. This is a quick
# look at the pilot data; the side-by-side figure with the original is in the Results.
if (nrow(keep) > 0) {
  keep |>
    group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(worried, na.rm = TRUE),
              se = sd(worried, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n)) |>   # standard error = SD / sqrt(n)
    ggplot(aes(x = condition, y = mean)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#1E6E76", width = 0.5) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), width = 0.15) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 5)) +                        # the scale goes from 1 to 5
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean worry (1-5), 95% CI",
         title = "Pilot A: worry by condition") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}
```

## Results

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are done by the shared
analysis code under Key statistics (open "Show the analysis code"). Describe anything you did to
the data beyond that.
:::

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The confirmatory test: worried, distress vs normal.
res_key <- key_result(phase1)
if (!is.null(res_key)) {
  res_key |>
    transmute(N, Beta = round(beta, 3), SE = round(se, 3), z = round(z, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Ordinal logistic regression: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry.")
} else {
  message("The model was not fitted: it needs at least 20 analysed participants, in at least two conditions.")
}

# The other outcomes, with the same model (secondary analyses), next to the original.
res_all <- all_results(phase1)
if (!is.null(res_all)) {
  res_all |>
    left_join(original |> select(outcome, orig_beta = beta, orig_se = se), by = "outcome") |>
    transmute(Outcome = outcome,
              `Original beta (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", orig_beta, orig_se),
              `Replication beta (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", beta, se),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Secondary outcomes: distress vs normal, same model as the key test.")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_row
rep  <- key_result(phase1)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Effect (beta)` = sprintf("%.3f", beta),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry (ordinal logistic beta).")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: the model needs at least 20 analysed participants in at least two conditions.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$beta >= rep$ci_low & orig$beta <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.3f. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$beta))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Effect of distress vs normal posts on each outcome, original study and Phase 1 replication (ordinal logistic beta). Bars are 95% confidence intervals. Positive means the distress group rated higher."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original, `Phase 1: replication` = all_results(phase1))
```

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the
demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
#| eval: false
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2

p1_counts <- if (have_data) risky_counts(phase1)
p1_stats  <- if (have_data) diff_ci(p1_counts)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(gain = p1_counts$risky[p1_counts$condition == "gain"] / p1_counts$n[p1_counts$condition == "gain"],
       loss = p1_counts$risky[p1_counts$condition == "loss"] / p1_counts$n[p1_counts$condition == "loss"],
       source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(gain = original_p_gain, loss = original_p_loss, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the difference at n per condition.
half_width <- function(n) 1.96 * sqrt(basis$gain * (1 - basis$gain) / n + basis$loss * (1 - basis$loss) / n)
power_at <- function(n, p1, p2) {
  tryCatch(power.prop.test(n = n, p1 = p1, p2 = p2, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.0f points", 100 * (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.0f points (expected)", 100 * half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.0f points", 100 * (original_p_loss - original_p_gain)),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.0f points", 100 * p1_stats$estimate),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.0f points", 50 * (original_p_loss - original_p_gain))),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_p_gain, original_p_loss),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, basis$gain, basis$loss),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_p_gain, original_p_gain + (original_p_loss - original_p_gain) / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per condition, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))
```
